items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up.

Agenda statement given but never confirmed. 'I'll ask you a bunch of questions about the move itself and within about ten minutes or so I should have an estimate built out here for you' is a real roadmap — and then no 'sound good?', no pause, no confirmation. The customer's only response was a confused 'For the meeting?' which went unaddressed.

The name discrepancy was never resolved. He asked 'What is your first and last name?' and got 'Viviana Gonzales,' but the Dialpad speaker on the line is Gustavo Taborga. He never clarified who he was speaking with versus whose move it is, never asked whether the person on the phone is authorized to book, and then referenced neither name again. At the close the customer said 'can you please send the code so I can see you later with my husband' — so there is a third party in the decision, and Garrison now has a quote going to an email he never read back, for a household whose decision-maker structure he never mapped.

Floors and stairs never asked at either end. The destination — 8513 Dong Drive in Austin — was never characterized at all. House or apartment? One story or three? Stairs? He built and priced a move without knowing where the boxes are going once the truck arrives.
Packing needs never asked. Thirty boxes and a mattress sitting in a father-in-law's garage, and he never asked whether they're actually packed and sealed or whether the customer needs help.
Special considerations never probed — no long walks, narrow hallways, tight turns, low branches.

Moving-stressor question never asked.

On a call where he told the customer they might finish in an hour and a half, the proration is the whole answer to 'what happens if we run past two and a half?' and it was never given.

No sense-check anywhere. The pricing and clock block ran roughly 400 words with no 'does that make sense?' — and the evidence that it didn't land is in the transcript: the customer had to interrupt and re-ask the central number, 'So, two hours and two hours and a half. Sorry, two hours and a half, it's minimum, like 200. How much did you say?'

No typical time range for the job. He never said what a load like this normally takes. He quoted the minimum — $520 for two and a half hours — and said 'I do expect this' before being cut off, and then never came back to it. The customer walked away with a floor price and no actual estimate.

Drive time never factored. North Austin to South Austin is a real cross-town haul and it never entered the pricing, the estimate, or a trip-fee discussion. Whether this move is inside the free service zone was never established or stated.
Traffic never mentioned on a cross-town Austin move.
Walk distance never asked — garage to curb at origin, curb to house at destination.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used to make the hours concrete.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. And the setup was handed to him: the entire load is thirty boxes and a mattress already sitting in a two-car garage. 'Have everything stacked by the garage door before we get there' is a thirty-second tip that meaningfully changes a job this small, and it never came.

Zero booking attempt. The customer said 'can you please send the code so I can see you later with my husband' — an explicit buying signal with a named decision step — and Garrison's entire response was to promise an email and add 'whenever you are ready.' No offer to hold Tuesday the 15th, no 'want me to pencil it in?', no follow-up time proposed. He had already confirmed availability on that date at the top of the call and never used it.

No BOLDED-list framing and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. 'You can even respond directly to that email' was offered for questions, not for verifying the details — and on a call with an unresolved name discrepancy and an unread-back email address, verification is exactly what was needed.
Hours and how to reach us never given.
Customer's name used zero times. Not once in six minutes and forty seconds — which is partly downstream of never resolving which name to use.
Insurance never explained. No 60c/lb baseline, no comparison, nothing the customer could take into a competing quote.
top_strength: Garrison's no-hidden-fees pitch is the sharpest of the eight calls, and it is the rubric bullet most reps deliver as a shrug. He doesn't just claim inclusion, he pre-empts the specific fees the customer will see on the next quote they get: 'absolutely everything is included within that hourly rate so that's gonna mean, fuel truck taxes, insurance, all moving blanket, shrink wrapped all these four wheelers all that good stuff... So just know there are no additional fees cost or charges of any type with us. So no, none of the constant ones in the moving industry things like credit card fees, fuel fees, truck fees, [heavy] item fees, et cetera.' Naming them as 'the constant ones in the moving industry' is the move — it arms the customer to spot them elsewhere. His hourly rate framing is also the textbook version and the only fully correct one this week: '$104 per mover per hour we would send up two movers in a case like this so we'd be looking at $208 an hour for the two of them.' Per mover, per hour, then the team math — that is how the rate should be stated every time, and most of the sample gives the team number only. He handled the minimum with unusual honesty rather than hiding behind it: 'if we were to complete this move within say an hour and a half which admittedly we very well might we do still have to bill for two and a half hours worth of work regardless which is in the amount of $520,' then immediately turned it into a certainty the customer could act on — 'we don't have any additional [fees] cost or charges, not even taxes. So, that $520 is quite literally the number that you would walk away with.' Telling a customer the job will likely take less time than they're paying for, before they ask, is a trust move. He also caught a bad data point in the record and cleared it fast — 'regarding that stoves lane address that's showing as a storage unit, is that correct?' produced 'it's my [father] in-law house but everything is on his garage' — and then followed up intelligently with the garage-fullness question ('how full as a percentage? Would you say that garage is with your items? 100 percent being like front to back [floor] to ceiling'), which is a genuinely good way to size an unseen load. And when the customer interrupted with the one thing actually on his mind — 'are you gonna specify the size of the truck in there?' — Garrison answered it fully and reassuringly on the spot: 'our truck size will be way more than enough. It's a 26 foot box truck. So, so it'll be certainly sufficient to fit absolutely everything within it.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: this call had the clearest buying signal of the week and no booking attempt at all. 'Can you please send the code so I can see you later with my husband' is a customer telling you exactly what the last step is, and Garrison answered it with an email and 'whenever you are ready.' He had already confirmed availability on Tuesday the 15th in the first thirty seconds — 'looks like we do have availability on that date at this time here' — and then never spent it. The line he needed: 'Absolutely, I'll get that over to you now. And since there's no deposit and nothing on a card, let me go ahead and hold Tuesday the fifteenth for you while you two talk — it costs you nothing, and if you decide against it you just reply to the email and I'll release it. That way the date's yours instead of going to whoever calls next.' No deposit was mentioned on this call, but as a fact at the end rather than as the tool that removes the risk of saying yes today. Second priority: he quoted a floor, not an estimate. Every other rep this week gave a typical range and landed a number inside it. Garrison gave only the minimum — $520 — and the one time he started toward an actual estimate ('but that said, I do expect this') he got cut off and never returned. A customer comparing quotes now has Einstein's number as a bare minimum against competitors' real estimates, which reads as either suspiciously cheap or incomplete. The fix: 'For a mattress and thirty boxes out of a garage, I'd expect us right at that two-and-a-half-hour minimum, maybe pushing three with the cross-town drive — so plan on $520 to around $625.' Third, this move has a whole half he never asked about. He knows everything about the garage and nothing about 8513 Dong Drive. House or apartment, stairs, parking, walk distance, whether anyone will be there — all unknown, all priced anyway. On a job this small, one flight of stairs at the destination is a meaningful percentage of the total hours. Fourth, the differentiators: zero for three. No Worries Damage Coverage, Meet Your Mover, and the On-Time Guarantee were all absent, and the whole block costs about sixty seconds. Fifth, resolve the name. He asked for a name, got 'Viviana Gonzales' from a caller whose line is Gustavo Taborga, never reconciled it, and then used no name at all for the rest of the call — which is why Section 8 loses a point and why the follow-up email may be going to the wrong person. 'Just so I've got the file right — am I speaking with Viviana, or are you calling on her behalf? And what's the best email for the quote?' takes five seconds. On estimate accuracy, no padding flag here; if anything the opposite risk — quoting the bare minimum on a job he never fully scoped means the first real variable that appears on move day shows up as an overage the customer wasn't prepared for, and an overage against a minimum reads worse to a customer than an overage against a range.
phone_presence_notes: Friendly and easy to talk to, with genuine energy in the truck-size answer and no defensiveness anywhere, but the warmth ran on autopilot — 'perfect, perfect,' 'gotcha, gotcha,' and 'alrighty' land repeatedly as filler rather than acknowledgment, the customer's name was never used once, and the customer had to stop him and re-ask the central price ('How much did you say?'), which suggests he was talking past rather than with.
audio_review_reason: The clarity-and-pace bullet was deducted on the strength of one exchange — the customer interrupting to re-ask the rate, then repeating it back twice to confirm ('520 for two hours and a half') — and the transcript can't distinguish the two explanations. Either Garrison delivered a 400-word pricing block too fast to follow, which is coachable, or the customer is working in a second language (the transcript shows non-native phrasing throughout: 'it's not a story hit. It's my Fath in-law house but everything is on his garage') and needed a slower, more checked-in delivery, which is a different coaching conversation. Audio would also settle the name discrepancy between the stated caller and the Dialpad speaker.
